results.title: payment-service → subscription-wide Contributor role
results.narrative: payment-service → subscription-wide Contributor role. Why it matters: A compromised payment-service container/process could use its Contributor role to read, modify, or delete ANY resource in the subscription — not just the ones it actually needs. If left as-is: Full subscription compromise from a single workload breach. Fix: Replace with a custom role scoped to exactly the resource(s) payment-service needs (see modules/iam's custom role_definition pattern).

results.title: customer-db allows public network access
results.narrative: customer-db allows public network access. Why it matters: customer-db is reachable directly from the internet, bypassing every network control. If left as-is: Direct exposure of customer data to internet-wide scanning and exploitation. Fix: Set public_network_access_enabled = false and add a private endpoint in the data subnet.

results.title: customer-storage allows public blob/container access
results.narrative: customer-storage allows public blob/container access. Why it matters: Any container in customer-storage could be individually set to public, exposing its contents with a URL. If left as-is: Silent data exposure — no network log will show it as unusual, it's 'working as configured'. Fix: Disable public nested-item access at the account level so no container can opt in later.

results.title: No network segmentation in trust boundary 'flat'
results.narrative: No network segmentation in trust boundary 'flat'. Why it matters: Compute workloads and sensitive data stores share one flat network zone. A single compromised container can reach every data store here directly — this is the exact 'payment service → unrestricted database access' pattern. If left as-is: Lateral movement from any one compromised service to all sensitive data. Fix: Split into dedicated subnets (see modules/network's gateway/aks/data/mgmt layout) with deny-by-default NSGs.

results.title: customer-db has no encryption at rest
results.narrative: customer-db has no encryption at rest. Why it matters: Data in customer-db is readable/tamperable by anyone with disk-level or backup access. If left as-is: Regulatory exposure (data protection requirements) plus tampering risk on backups/snapshots. Fix: Enable encryption at rest (see the require-encryption-at-rest Azure Policy in modules/policy).

results.title: No centralized audit logging configured
results.narrative: No centralized audit logging configured. Why it matters: Without diagnostic logs flowing to a central workspace, there's no way to reconstruct what happened after an incident, or prove who did what. If left as-is: Undetectable breaches and no forensic trail — also a compliance gap (most frameworks require audit logging). Fix: Wire up diagnostic settings + a Log Analytics workspace (Phase 9 — SIEM + Detection, not yet built).

results.title: notification-service has no dedicated identity/role
results.narrative: notification-service has no dedicated identity/role. Why it matters: notification-service reaches sensitive data with no assigned identity. In practice this gets worked around with a shared service account, an ambient credential, or a manually-granted broad role — all worse than a scoped one from the start. If left as-is: No way to attribute or limit this workload's access; likely over-privileged in practice. Fix: Create a dedicated app registration/service principal and custom role for notification-service, matching payment-service's pattern.

results.title: No application-layer authentication: api-gateway → payment-service
results.narrative: No application-layer authentication: api-gateway → payment-service. Why it matters: Network reachability from api-gateway to payment-service exists, but there's no app-layer proof of identity (mTLS/OAuth/service-mesh token) — anything else that lands in the same subnet can impersonate the caller. If left as-is: Any workload placed in the same network path can call this service as if it were the legitimate caller. Fix: Introduce a service mesh (mTLS) or OAuth token validation between gateway and services (Phase 4 — Zero Trust).

results.title: api-gateway has no WAF/rate-limiting in front of it
results.narrative: api-gateway has no WAF/rate-limiting in front of it. Why it matters: api-gateway is directly internet-facing with no layer-7 filtering — vulnerable to L7 DoS and common injection patterns hitting the app directly. If left as-is: Availability risk and a missing layer of defense against common web attacks. Fix: Deploy Azure Front Door or Application Gateway with a WAF policy in front of the gateway subnet.

results.title: Deployment/payment-service container 'payment-service' runs privileged
results.narrative: Deployment/payment-service container 'payment-service' runs privileged. Why it matters: A privileged container has essentially unrestricted access to the host — every device, every kernel capability, no seccomp/AppArmor confinement. A compromised process inside it can escape to the node directly. If left as-is: Container compromise becomes node compromise, and from there every workload scheduled on that node. Fix: Remove privileged: true; request only the specific capabilities actually needed instead (see K8S-CAP-01).

results.title: Deployment/account-service shares the host's hostNetwork, hostPID
results.narrative: Deployment/account-service shares the host's hostNetwork, hostPID. Why it matters: hostNetwork exposes the node's real network interfaces (no namespace isolation — the pod sees and can inject on the same interfaces the node itself uses); hostPID/hostIPC let the pod see and signal every process on the node, not just its own. If left as-is: A compromised pod can sniff/spoof node-level network traffic and inspect or kill other pods' processes on the same node. Fix: Remove the hostNetwork/hostPID/hostIPC fields; use a Kubernetes Service for network access and standard pod-to-pod isolation instead.

results.title: ClusterRole/payment-service-role grants wildcard verbs and resources ('*'/'*')
results.narrative: ClusterRole/payment-service-role grants wildcard verbs and resources ('*'/'*'). Why it matters: Any ServiceAccount bound to this role can read, create, modify, or delete any resource of any kind cluster-wide — Secrets, other workloads' pods, RBAC objects themselves. If left as-is: A compromised pod using this identity can pivot to read every Secret and take over every other workload it can reach, not just act within its own intended scope. Fix: Replace the wildcard rule with the specific verbs and resources the bound ServiceAccount actually needs — same least-privilege principle as the cloud IAM roles in terraform/*/modules/iam.

results.title: Deployment/account-service container 'account-service' does not enforce runAsNonRoot
results.narrative: Deployment/account-service container 'account-service' does not enforce runAsNonRoot. Why it matters: Without runAsNonRoot: true, the container can run as UID 0 (root) — whatever the image's Dockerfile happens to specify, not a property this manifest actually controls. If left as-is: A container-breakout bug is far more dangerous as root: it starts with root's filesystem/capability defaults instead of an unprivileged user's. Fix: Add runAsNonRoot: true (and runAsUser: <non-zero UID>) to the container's securityContext.

results.title: Deployment/account-service container 'account-service' does not drop all Linux capabilities
results.narrative: Deployment/account-service container 'account-service' does not drop all Linux capabilities. Why it matters: Containers get a broad default capability set unless the manifest explicitly drops it. Most workloads need none of the default set at all. If left as-is: An unnecessary default capability (e.g. CAP_NET_RAW, CAP_CHOWN) becomes one more tool available to an attacker who compromises the process. Fix: Add capabilities.drop: ["ALL"] and only capabilities.add the specific ones the workload actually requires, if any.

results.title: Namespace 'app' has workloads but no NetworkPolicy
results.narrative: Namespace 'app' has workloads but no NetworkPolicy. Why it matters: With no NetworkPolicy, Kubernetes' default is allow-all: every pod in the cluster can reach every pod in this namespace on any port, regardless of whether the service mesh's mTLS (modules/mesh) is proving who's calling. If left as-is: A compromised pod anywhere in the cluster — not just this namespace — can reach every workload here directly, enabling lateral movement the mesh's identity layer alone doesn't prevent. Fix: Add a default-deny-all NetworkPolicy for the namespace, then explicit allow rules scoped to each workload's real traffic pattern (see kubernetes/manifests/hardened/networkpolicy.yaml).

results.title: Deployment/notification-service container 'notification-service' has no cpu/memory limit
results.narrative: Deployment/notification-service container 'notification-service' has no cpu/memory limit. Why it matters: Without resource limits, one runaway or compromised container can consume all available CPU/memory on its node, starving every other pod scheduled there. If left as-is: A single misbehaving or intentionally resource-exhausting container becomes a node-wide (and potentially cluster-wide, via rescheduling pressure) denial of service. Fix: Add resources.requests and resources.limits (both cpu and memory) sized to the workload's actual usage.

results.title: Deployment/notification-service container 'notification-service' uses a mutable image reference (meridiantrustbank/notification-service:latest)
results.narrative: Deployment/notification-service container 'notification-service' uses a mutable image reference (meridiantrustbank/notification-service:latest). Why it matters: ':latest' (or no tag at all) can point to different actual image content on different days, or even different content on the same tag if it gets re-pushed — there's no way to know exactly what code is running, or to roll back to a known-good build reliably. If left as-is: An attacker (or a mistake) that re-pushes the same tag changes what every future pod runs without any manifest change to review or audit. Fix: Pin the image to a specific version (and ideally a content digest, e.g. image@sha256:...) produced by CI, not a floating tag.

results.title: customer-storage drifted to allow public network access (baseline had it disabled)
results.narrative: customer-storage drifted to allow public network access (baseline had it disabled). Why it matters: customer-storage's live configuration now allows public network access, but the last-known-good baseline it was provisioned with had this disabled — the resource was changed outside of, or after, the change that was actually reviewed. If left as-is: Direct exposure of a sensitive resource, introduced silently after go-live rather than caught at design time. Fix: Investigate who/what changed customer-storage's network exposure and revert to the baseline configuration; consider Azure Policy/Org Policy/AWS Config in enforce (not audit-only) mode to block this class of change going forward.

results.title: account-service's identity binding drifted from baseline
results.narrative: account-service's identity binding drifted from baseline. Why it matters: account-service was provisioned with role='IAM-004-account-service-secrets-access' scope='resource'; the current snapshot shows role='Owner' scope='subscription'. If left as-is: An identity's actual permissions no longer match what was reviewed — the exact kind of change that should go through an access review, not happen silently. Fix: Confirm whether this was an approved change; if not, revert account-service's binding to the baseline role/scope and investigate how it changed.

results.title: key-vault drifted to no longer have encryption at rest
results.narrative: key-vault drifted to no longer have encryption at rest. Why it matters: key-vault was provisioned with encryption at rest enabled; the current snapshot shows it disabled. If left as-is: Data at rest is now readable/tamperable by anyone with disk-level or backup access, without that ever having been reviewed as an intended change. Fix: Re-enable encryption at rest and investigate how/why it was disabled outside the reviewed baseline.

results.title: Centralized audit logging drifted from enabled to disabled
results.narrative: Centralized audit logging drifted from enabled to disabled. Why it matters: Logging was on in the reviewed baseline and is off in the current snapshot — anything that changes after this point (including further drift) may go completely unrecorded. If left as-is: Total loss of forensic trail from this point forward; every other drift or intrusion after this one becomes harder or impossible to reconstruct. Fix: Re-enable diagnostic settings/audit logging immediately and treat this as a potential incident, not just a misconfiguration — investigate who disabled it and when.

results.title: debug-endpoint appears in the current snapshot but not in the reviewed baseline
results.narrative: debug-endpoint appears in the current snapshot but not in the reviewed baseline. Why it matters: debug-endpoint (type=api) exists in the live/current configuration with no corresponding entry in the last reviewed baseline — either an out-of-band provisioning action or a baseline that's fallen out of date. If left as-is: An unreviewed resource in the environment — potentially a legitimate change nobody updated the baseline for, or a genuinely unauthorized/shadow resource. Either way, nobody has assessed its security posture. Fix: Confirm whether debug-endpoint was an approved change. If yes, update the baseline architecture.json to include it and run the threat-modelling agent against the updated design. If no, treat this as a potential incident.

results.title: Authentication drifted off on api-gateway → account-service
results.narrative: Authentication drifted off on api-gateway → account-service. Why it matters: api-gateway → account-service was mutually authenticated in the baseline; the current snapshot shows it is not. If left as-is: Zero Trust protection on this path has silently regressed — anything reachable on the network path can now impersonate the legitimate caller. Fix: Investigate the mesh/gateway configuration on this path for a dropped PeerAuthentication policy or misconfigured sidecar, and restore mutual authentication.

results.title: notification-service is in the reviewed baseline but missing from the current snapshot
results.narrative: notification-service is in the reviewed baseline but missing from the current snapshot. Why it matters: notification-service (type=compute) was part of the last reviewed baseline and no longer appears in the current configuration. If left as-is: Either a legitimate decommission the baseline hasn't caught up with yet, or an unexpected/unauthorized deletion — for a logging or data asset specifically, deletion can itself be an attempt to remove evidence. Fix: Confirm whether notification-service's removal was intentional. If yes, update the baseline architecture.json to drop it. If no, treat this as a potential incident — especially if notification-service handled logging or sensitive data.

results.title: 5 failed logins for k.doran from 185.220.101.4, followed by a success
results.narrative: 5 failed logins for k.doran from 185.220.101.4, followed by a success. What happened: 5 consecutive authentication failures for k.doran from 185.220.101.4, then a successful login from the same IP — consistent with a guessed or stuffed credential that worked. Why it matters: Likely account takeover — treat the account as compromised until verified otherwise. Recommended action: Force a password/credential reset, review MFA status, and rate-limit or block the source IP.

results.title: k.doran transferred 950 MB from customer-storage
results.narrative: k.doran transferred 950 MB from customer-storage. What happened: k.doran moved 950 MB out of customer-storage in a single transfer at 2026-09-17T01:31:47Z — well above the 500 MB baseline for normal activity. Why it matters: Large single-transfer volumes from a sensitive store are the single strongest signal of bulk data exfiltration, insider or external. Recommended action: Suspend k.doran's active sessions pending review, and confirm the transfer against a known, approved business process.

results.title: k.doran disabled audit logging on log-workspace
results.narrative: k.doran disabled audit logging on log-workspace. What happened: k.doran disabled logging on log-workspace at 2026-09-17T01:40:02Z. Why it matters: Tampering with the audit trail is a near-universal signal of an active, deliberate attack — it removes the evidence needed to investigate everything else. Recommended action: Treat as an active incident immediately: re-enable/restore logging, isolate k.doran's credentials, and escalate — do not wait for corroborating alerts.

results.title: After-hours privilege change by k.doran on secrets-manager-role
results.narrative: After-hours privilege change by k.doran on secrets-manager-role. What happened: k.doran granted/changed permissions on secrets-manager-role at 2026-09-17T01:22:10Z (outside 06:00-22:00 UTC business hours). Why it matters: Off-hours IAM changes to sensitive resources are a common early step in both insider misuse and post-compromise privilege escalation. Recommended action: Confirm this change against an approved change ticket; if none exists, revert it and investigate k.doran.
